title: Fanout proxy impact on tail latency — field notes and microbenchmarks
content:
Purpose:
Quick notes and initial benchmark results exploring how fanout through edge proxies (L7 ingress that fans a single client request to multiple backend streams) changes tail-percentile latency under realistic streaming and chunked-response workloads. Trying to isolate whether tail effects are dominated by: client-side connection concurrency, proxy request multiplexing, TLS proxy serialization points, or backend KV-cache warmup interactions.

Motivation / why this matters:
- We observe intermittent P99 spikes for hosted API customers when routes enable: proxy fanout, streaming responses, or backend bursty kv-warm conditions.
- SLOs are p50<30ms, p95<120ms, p99<350ms for non-streaming generation paths. Streaming endpoints intentionally accept higher medians; but tail behavior is unpredictable and causes customer incidents (see INF-1245).

Hypotheses (ordered by likeliness):
1) Proxy fanout increases head-of-line blocking because one slow backend stream stalls combined response serialization and delays final chunk commit.
2) TLS termination and re-encryption at the proxy creates scheduling jitter (TLS handshake reuse pressure) under high ephemeral-connection rates.
3) Multiplexing layer (HTTP/2 or gRPC) buffer sizes + chunk coalescing heuristics add variable delay when combining N backend chunks.
4) Client retries increase burstiness and interact poorly with proxy queueing disciplines.

Testbed overview (mini-journal):
- 3-node proxy cluster (haproxy/nginx-like config; our internal edge-proxy build).
- 6 backend worker instances (model-serving stub that streams 4 chunks total, chunk sizes configurable).
- Clients: 8 parallel load generators running vegeta + a custom streaming harness using grpc-go and curl-like tooling.
- Network conditions: baseline datacenter (10Gbps, no packet loss), and an injected 1ms/2% jitter scenario using tc netem for sensitivity tests.
- Observability: p50/p95/p99 at client-side, proxy egress queue latency, backend process queue depth histograms, TLS session reuse metrics.

Workloads tried (summary):
A) Small-chunk streaming: 6 chunks x 256B every 5–10ms (latency-sensitive chat-style).
B) Large-chunk streaming: 2 chunks x 64KB at 20ms (batch-style but streaming-enabled).
C) Unary fanout: single request fans to 3 backends (concurrent partial responses aggregated).
D) High-concurrency open-loop: 400 concurrent client connections, ~800 requests/s sustained.

Representative commands (local):
- vegeta: echo "GET /v1/stream" | vegeta attack -duration=60s -rate=150 | vegeta report
- streaming harness: go run ./cmd/stream-harness -target proxy:443 -concurrency=200 -fanout=3 -mode=grpc

Key measurements (concise table - median of 3 runs each):
- Workload A (small chunks): p50 45ms, p95 210ms, p99 780ms 
- Workload B (large chunks): p50 130ms, p95 380ms, p99 980ms
- Workload C (unary fanout 3x): p50 62ms, p95 410ms, p99 1250ms
- Workload D (high conc): p50 85ms, p95 670ms, p99 2100ms

Proxy-side telemetry observations:
- When fanout >1, serialization latency (time between last backend chunk arrival and first client byte) grows nonlinearly with fanout due to our proxy combining window (implemented to reduce tiny-packet amplification).
- TCP retransmits negligible in baseline; under netem jitter, P99 increases by ~1.8x for streaming small-chunk workloads.
- TLS sessions: ephemeral new TLS sessions per client increased CPU usage spikes on proxy leading to intermittent scheduling stalls (seen as blocked goroutines in our proxy build). Reuse reduces spikes dramatically.

Backend-side notes:
- KV-cache warm path: cold K/V lookups that complete inside the backend stream create stragglers that map directly to the overall P99 in fanout scenarios. Eg: 1 slow backend increases aggregated P99 by ~60% for fanout=3 because proxy waits for all pieces before final chunk (explicit aggregator semantics).
- Backpressure signal: our backends push with a fixed pacing to simulate generation; when the proxy buffers exceed threshold we see TCP pushback which cascades to increased scheduling delays in the worker event loop.

Microbench experiment: disable proxy combine-window (immediate passthrough) vs 5ms combine-window vs 20ms window
- Immediate passthrough: p99 down 35% for small-chunk streaming, but client saw increased packet count and slight bandwidth overhead.
- 5ms window: best tradeoff at moderate workloads; p95 similar to passthrough, p99 slightly higher (~10%).
- 20ms window: p99 worse by ~2x in most streaming configs.

Queueing/Multiplexing behavior notes:
- HTTP/2 streams: head-of-line scheduling in our proxy implementation currently favors in-order per-connection processing; a slow stream can delay subsequent streams when the proxy serializes writes over a shared connection.
- gRPC: unary fanout responses reassembled into a single response payload by the aggregator; the reassembly is susceptible to one-slow-backend problems.

Preliminary conclusions:
- The dominant contributors to tail in these experiments are: (1) aggregator semantics (waiting for all fanout parts), (2) proxy combine-window sizing, and (3) backend cold-path stragglers. TLS/handshake jitter is secondary but visible under high ephemeral connection rates.
- Good knobs: enable TLS session reuse, reduce combine-window from 20ms to 5ms for streaming-heavy routes, and add a per-backend slow-response threshold (cutoff and synthesize partial/placeholder chunk) to avoid single-straggler amplification.

Action items / next experiments:
- INF-1245 follow-up: test partial-aggregation strategy (timeout-per-backend 120ms) and measure P99 reduction (owner: Aisha).
- Implement server-side per-response deadlines and return partial responses when backend exceeds latency budget. Measure correctness impact for chat/structured outputs (owner: Diego).
- Run a long-run soak (24h) with TLS session reuse disabled vs enabled to quantify CPU/scheduling tail effects (owner: Liam).
- Investigate HTTP/2 stream scheduling change: allow out-of-order write for independent streams to reduce HOL blocking (RFC and safety review needed).

Open questions / risks:
- Partial aggregation semantics may break customers relying on strict completeness; need opt-in at route level.
- Bandwidth overhead tradeoffs for passthrough vs combine-window—will increase metered costs for some customers.
- On-prem/private deployments may have differing network characteristics; changes should be togglable per deployment mode.

Notes to self / loose thoughts:
- Add a simulation harness that can inject backend stragglers deterministically (we had a prototype, need to extend to fanout patterns).
- Consider integrating a small ML-based straggler predictor using recent per-request telemetry to pre-emptively decide whether to partial-aggregate. Probably overkill but interesting.

Raw logs and experiment artifacts: stored in s3://redwood-infra-bench/fanout-experiments/2026-11- (see linked PR for scripts).

References and related tickets:
- INF-1245: customer incident + initial triage notes
- PR 879: proxy combine-window change (WIP)
- Slack thread: #runtime-bench-discuss 2026-11-13 (initial cluster logs attached)

TL;DR (one-liner): Fanout through aggregating proxies amplifies single-backend stragglers into very large P99 spikes — short-term mitigations: lower combine-window, enable TLS reuse, and add per-backend cutoffs; longer-term: partial-aggregation and smarter stream scheduling.

Draft status: exploratory. Planning to run follow-ups and iterate on config knobs; will convert to a formal runbook if results hold across cloud regions.
